title: People, body, temple (CCC 781–810)
hook: three images for what the Church is

segments.voice: Yesterday, signs of the Spirit: water, oil, fire, cloud, seal, hand, finger, dove. Your line was fire and dove. Which one did you catch yourself seeing? Day one thousand eighty.

What is a church? Ask a child to draw one and you'll probably get a building: a pointed roof, a door, a cross on top. That's fair; it's what the word means on a street sign. But when the Catechism asks what the Church is, it doesn't draw a building first. It reaches for pictures, the way scripture does, and it gives several. This part of the Catechism gathers them around three: a people, a body, and a temple. Each one shows something the others miss. Today's word is the first.
screen: `A POINTED ROOF AND A DOOR.` → `NOT A BUILDING FIRST.` → `A PEOPLE, A BODY, A TEMPLE.`

segments.voice: People. The Catechism says God chose to make human beings holy not one by one, with no link between them, but as a people. The Catechism begins that story with Israel, the people God chose and made a covenant with, and reads the Church as growing out of it. The first letter of Peter says it to scattered believers, in the Douay-Rheims: "Who in time past were not a people: but are now the people of God." A people has a history, a memory, a road it's walking. The Catechism lists what marks this one: you join by faith and baptism, its law is love, its mission is to be salt and light, and its destination is the kingdom. Body. Paul writes to a quarrelsome church in Corinth: "Now you are the body of Christ, and members of member." A body is one thing made of very different parts. The eye can't tell the hand it has no need of it. Christ is the head, the Catechism says, and the members are joined to him and to each other; when one part suffers, all suffer. A people can drift apart. A body can't, not without bleeding. Temple. Paul again: "Know you not, that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" The Catechism quotes Saint Augustine here, and it echoes the lesson on body and soul. What the soul is to the human body, Augustine says, the Holy Spirit is to the body of Christ, the Church. So: a people on the move, a body joined together, a temple where God lives. One picture alone can tilt. A people without a body becomes a crowd; a body without the Spirit, a corpse; a temple without a people, an empty building.
screen: `PEOPLE: HOLY TOGETHER, NOT ALONE.` · `BODY: ONE THING, MANY PARTS.` · `TEMPLE: WHERE THE SPIRIT LIVES.` · `EACH PICTURE NEEDS THE OTHERS.` · then, large: `NOW THE PEOPLE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hold your parish, or your local church, in mind. Settle, and breathe. If you belong to a parish, see it from the back pew: the regulars, the family who's always late, the person at the door, the priest. If you don't belong to one, take the church nearest where you live, and the people who walk into it on Sunday. Let them be a people, a body, a house with someone home. If you pray, you can pray for them by name, or by face. If you don't, wish them well, one by one. The bell holds the time.
People. The first of the Catechism's three pictures of the Church: God's people, made holy together, alongside the body of Christ and the temple of the Spirit. Today's word.
Your line: three pictures. Today, the next time you pass a church building, say the three pictures over in your head: a people, a body, a temple. Day one thousand eighty.

howItsDone: Catholics pray for the Church and for their parish in the prayers of the faithful at Mass, and speak of the Church as the people of God, the body of Christ and the temple of the Holy Spirit.

original.note: the Greek word for "people" in 1 Peter 2:10, "now the people of God".

trapdoor: what you thought: the church is the building on the corner.
what it means: in Catholic teaching, the Church is a people, a body and a temple, all at once.
what a scholar hears: CCC 781–810, with Augustine's line that the Holy Spirit is to the Church what the soul is to the body.

notes: Confirm Challoner wording of 1 Peter 2:10, 1 Corinthians 12:27 and 1 Corinthians 3:16.

CCC paraphrased: holy as a people, not individually (781), marks of the people of God (782), body with Christ the head (787–795), Augustine on the Spirit as the soul of the Church (797), temple (797–798).

'The Church sees itself as that story's continuation, never its replacement of an old people with a new one' is written to avoid supersessionist framing (cf. CCC 839, Nostra Aetate 4). Keeper should check this sentence carefully; it goes slightly beyond CCC 781–810.
'Gathers them around three' follows the outline; the Catechism also uses other images (sheepfold, field, bride, mother).
Closing line ('a people without a body becomes a crowd…') is the writer's image, not the Catechism's.
Original: λαός, as in 'λαὸς θεοῦ' (1 Peter 2:10).

Editor: replaced a garbled sentence that went beyond the cited text ('never its replacement of an old people with a new one') with the Catechism's own Israel framing; the soul callback said 'earlier this week' though day 1072 was last week.
Audit: read in full; no changes. 1 Peter 2:10, 1 Corinthians 12:27 and 3:16 Challoner wording checked; Augustine (Sermon 267) correctly cited via CCC 797.
